To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) in some cases, ''correcting'' a positive example is better than receiving a negative (counter) example; (2) in some cases a negative example is better than access to the full positive data.

(1) in general, one can learn a concept from a teacher who only provides negative counterexamples, (2) in general, learning with negative counterexamples and correcting positive examples is easier than learning with positive examples, (3) learning with positive examples is easier when the learner is allowed to query the teacher for the nearest positive example.
(1) one-shot learning is possible, (2) one-shot learning with negative counterexamples is possible, (3) one-shot learning from corrected positive examples is possible.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of formalizing learning from positive and negative examples and with the problem of comparing different learning models.
a question of how a learner can use the information about what is not correct in a language, in addition to information about what is correct.
formalization of learning languages from positive and negative evidence.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the best way to learn is to get corrected positive examples.
the most helpful type of evidence depends on the type of the target concept.
, in the context of one-shot learners, the best way to teach a child is to give her positive examples and then to correct them if she makes a mistake.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a one-shot learner with access to a teacher who is willing to provide both negative counterexamples and corrected positive examples can achieve the same learning capabilities as a one-shot learner who can query the teacher for full positive and negative examples.
, in some cases, the learner can be more successful with a limited amount of data, but with a more complex learning model.

a learner can learn a concept from one-shot examples, even if the learner has access only to the teacher's corrections of positive examples, or even if the teacher does not correct any positive example but provides only negative ones.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in the process learning, a child may be able to learn a language with fewer queries than it would take to learn the same language without the help of a teacher, or with the help of a different type of teacher.
the formalization of overt negative evidence and overt and covert positive evidence is possible within the framework of subset and membership queries.
the learner's access to the teacher (oracle) in the form of corrected or corrected and rephrased positive examples may be crucial in some cases for learning.
